paragraphs.heading: A military order
paragraphs.text: The Knights Templar were a Catholic military order, one of the most important in Western Christianity. In full they were the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of Solomon's Temple. The order lasted nearly two hundred years in the Middle Ages, and its knights, in white mantles with a red cross, were among the best fighters of the Crusades.

paragraphs.heading: Guarding the pilgrim roads
paragraphs.text: After the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, many Christians travelled to holy sites in the region. The city itself was fairly safe, but bandits on the road inland from the coast at Jaffa often killed pilgrims, sometimes hundreds at a time. In 1119 a French knight, Hugues de Payens, asked King Baldwin II and the Patriarch of Jerusalem to approve a religious order to protect them. The king agreed and gave the knights a headquarters in the captured Al-Aqsa Mosque on the Temple Mount, a site believed to lie above the ruins of Solomon's Temple.

paragraphs.heading: From poverty to power
paragraphs.text: At first there were only about nine knights, and they lived on donations. Their emblem, two knights sharing one horse, showed how poor they were. That changed when Bernard of Clairvaux, a leading churchman, championed them, and in 1129 the Council of Troyes gave the order the Church's formal approval. Money, land and recruits then poured in from families across Christendom. In 1139 a papal decree freed the Templars from local laws, so they could cross borders, pay no taxes and answer only to the pope.

paragraphs.heading: On the battlefield
paragraphs.text: In major battles the Templars often struck first: their heavily armoured knights charged on warhorses into enemy lines before the main army. At Montgisard in 1177, some 500 of them helped several thousand foot soldiers defeat Saladin's army of more than 26,000. Yet fighters were a minority of the order. Most members worked in support roles, looking after the knights and the order's finances.

paragraphs.heading: An early kind of bank
paragraphs.text: From 1150 the Templars issued letters of credit to pilgrims. A pilgrim left valuables at a local Templar house, received a document showing their worth, and claimed the same value on reaching the Holy Land. This kept travellers safe from robbers and also made the order richer, and it was an early form of banking. The Templars came to own farms, vineyards, ships and at one point the whole island of Cyprus.

paragraphs.heading: The fall
paragraphs.text: The order was closely bound to the Crusades, and once it could no longer hold its lands in the Holy Land, support for it faded. In 1307 King Philip IV of France had many Templars in France arrested and tortured into false confessions, and they were burned at the stake. Under pressure from Philip, Pope Clement V dissolved the order in 1312.
